label: Combinatorial 2-Complexes
notes: This appendix to section I.8 turns a group presentation into a two-dimensional space whose loops remember relations. Across printed pages 153 to 156 we build the presentation complex, recognise its fundamental group, pass to the Cayley 2-complex as universal cover, and read words off van Kampen diagrams before metrising each cell.

label: What is a combinatorial 2-complex
notes: A combinatorial 2-complex is built from vertices, oriented edges, and polygonal 2-cells attached along edge paths by combinatorial maps. We insist attaching maps send edges to edges so every gluing is bookkeeping on words. This discrete framing lets the same object be inspected as a space, as a group, and later as a metric object.

label: Group presentations
notes: A presentation packages a group as generators modulo relators. Each generator names an edge, each relator names a word that must equal the identity. Remind students that many groups share a presentation and that the relators, read as boundary words, are exactly the data we will glue two-cells along in the next slide.

label: The presentation 2-complex
notes: The presentation complex has a single vertex, one oriented loop per generator, and one polygonal 2-cell per relator glued along the boundary word spelled by that relator. Stress that traversing the cell boundary reads the relator letter by letter, so the geometry literally encodes the algebra of the presentation.

label: Fundamental group theorem
notes: By van Kampen's theorem the fundamental group of the presentation complex is exactly the presented group. The wedge of generator loops gives a free group; each attached two-cell kills its boundary word. Emphasise that this is the bridge making topology of the complex equivalent to algebra of the group.

label: The Cayley 2-complex
notes: The universal cover of the presentation complex is the Cayley 2-complex. Its one-skeleton is the Cayley graph, vertices are group elements, and lifted two-cells fill every loop spelling a relator. It is simply connected, and the group acts freely and cocompactly by deck transformations permuting the cells.

label: Words and cellular paths
notes: A word in the generators is an edge path from the basepoint; reduce by removing backtracks. The word represents the identity exactly when its path lifts to a loop in the Cayley complex. This reframes the word problem as a question about whether a closed path bounds inside the two-dimensional complex.

label: Van Kampen diagrams
notes: A van Kampen diagram is a planar, simply connected complex mapped combinatorially into the presentation complex, tiled by relator polygons, whose boundary spells the given word. Such a diagram exists precisely when the word equals the identity, so the diagram is a finite combinatorial certificate of that fact.

label: Reading a diagram
notes: Walk the example diagram: interior two-cells are relator copies, interior edges cancel in pairs, and the outer boundary reads the trivial word after free reduction. Point out that the number of two-cells used measures area, the combinatorial cost of proving the word trivial, foreshadowing isoperimetric functions.

label: Metrising the cells
notes: Give each polygonal two-cell the metric of an M_k polygon so the complex becomes a geodesic M_k-complex. Edge lengths and corner angles are now genuine geometric data, and the same combinatorial object carries a length metric in which we can finally ask about local curvature.

label: Link condition and curvature
notes: By the link condition the metric complex is locally CAT(k) exactly when every vertex link is a metric graph with no short loops, girth at least two-pi for k at most zero. Thus a presentation becomes non-positively curved when its links are large, linking algebra to global geometry.

label: Recap and outlook
notes: Recap the chain: presentation, presentation complex, fundamental group, Cayley complex, van Kampen diagram, metric and link condition. The payoff is that combinatorial group theory and non-positive curvature meet on one object. Diagrams are working records, and each picture is paired with an invariant the reader can check.
